hints: Look at the oxygen numbers first. It rises from 5 kPa in the pulmonary artery to 15 kPa in the pulmonary vein, so the blood must be gaining oxygen on this trip.
Remember where pulmonary vessels go. The pulmonary artery takes blood to the lungs and the pulmonary vein brings it back, so think about which way oxygen diffuses at the alveoli.
walkthrough:
**Trace the pulmonary route**

Think of the journey. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs. The pulmonary vein carries blood back from the lungs to the heart.

So anything that changes between these two vessels happens in the lungs.

**Read what happens to oxygen**

In the pulmonary artery, oxygen is low at $5 \text{ kPa}$. In the pulmonary vein, oxygen is high at $15 \text{ kPa}$.

That is a clear gain of oxygen. The blood has been oxygenated.

**Link the gain to diffusion at the alveoli**

In the lung capillaries, alveolar air has a higher partial pressure of oxygen than the incoming blood. Oxygen therefore diffuses down its concentration gradient from the alveoli into the blood.

This loading explains why the pulmonary vein leaves the lungs with much more oxygen.

options.A: Correct. Oxygen diffuses from the high partial pressure in the alveoli into the low partial pressure in the pulmonary capillary blood, raising oxygen from 5 to 15 kPa.
options.B: False. Carbon dioxide loss from blood to alveoli explains the fall in carbon dioxide from 6 to 5 kPa, not the rise in oxygen.
options.C: False. This describes tissue capillaries in the body, not pulmonary vessels, and oxygen moves from blood to body cells, not the other way.
options.D: False. This describes tissue capillaries in the body, not the lungs, and carbon dioxide moves from body cells into blood, not into cells.
